title: Dolphins: Smart Swimmers
summary: How dolphins breathe air, raise their calves, hunt as a team, find food with echoes, call each other by whistles, sleep with half the brain, and why they need a clean sea.
poll: Dolphins are smarter than most other sea animals.

versions.title: Dolphins in the Sea
versions.text:
Look at the sea. See the fin? It is a dolphin!

A dolphin lives in the sea. But it is not a fish. It is a mammal. So are you.

A dolphin needs air. It swims up to the top. It has a hole on its head. It is a blowhole. Air goes in. Air goes out.

A baby dolphin is a calf. It drinks milk from its mom. It stays with her for years.

Dolphins live in a group. It is a pod. The pod hunts fish as a team.

A dolphin makes clicks. The clicks hit a fish. They bounce back. That is an echo. Now the dolphin knows where the fish is.

Each dolphin has its own whistle. It is like a name.

How does a dolphin sleep? Half of its brain rests. One eye stays open.

Dolphins swim in the Red Sea. But nets can hurt them. Trash can hurt them, too. Let us keep the sea clean.

versions.title: Dolphins: Smart Swimmers
versions.text:
Look out at the sea on a calm day. You may see a fin cut through the waves. Then a dolphin jumps into the air!

Dolphins live in the sea, but they are not fish. They are mammals, just like people. Mammals breathe air, and their babies drink milk.

A dolphin must swim up to the top of the water to breathe. It has a hole on top of its head called a blowhole. The dolphin pushes old air out and takes new air in. Then it dives down again.

A baby dolphin is called a calf. The calf drinks milk from its mother. It stays close to her for three years or more.

Dolphins live in groups called pods. The dolphins in a pod help each other. Sometimes they swim in a circle around fish to trap them.

Dolphins can find food without seeing it. A dolphin sends out quick clicks. The clicks hit a fish and bounce back as an echo. The echo tells the dolphin where the fish is.

Each dolphin also has its own special whistle. Other dolphins use it like a name.

Dolphins sleep in a strange way. Only half of the brain rests at a time. One eye often stays open.

Dolphins live in the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf. But fishing nets and plastic trash can hurt them. Keeping the sea clean helps dolphins stay safe.

versions.title: Dolphins: Smart Swimmers
versions.text:
On a calm morning, a gray fin cuts through the waves. Then a sleek animal leaps high into the air and splashes back down. It is a dolphin, one of the smartest animals in the sea.

Dolphins live in the ocean, but they are not fish. They are mammals, like people. Mammals breathe air, and their babies drink milk from their mothers.

Because it needs air, a dolphin must swim up to the surface again and again. It breathes through a blowhole on the top of its head. With one quick puff, it blows out old air and takes in fresh air. Then it dives down again.

A baby dolphin is called a calf. Right after it is born, its mother helps it reach the surface for its first breath. The calf drinks her milk and stays with her for three to six years.

Dolphins live in groups called pods. The members of a pod work together. They may swim in a circle around a group of fish to trap them.

Dolphins can find food even in dark or cloudy water. A dolphin sends out fast clicks. When the clicks hit a fish, they bounce back as an echo. The echo tells the dolphin where the fish is and how big it is.

Each dolphin also has its own special whistle. Other dolphins use this whistle like a name.

Dolphins sleep in an unusual way. Only half of the brain rests at a time, and one eye often stays open. That way, the dolphin can keep breathing and watch for danger.

Dolphins live in the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf. However, fishing nets and plastic trash can hurt them. Keeping the sea clean helps them stay safe.

versions.title: Dolphins: Smart Swimmers
versions.text:
On a calm morning in the Red Sea, a gray fin slices through the waves. A moment later, a sleek animal leaps high into the air and splashes back down. It is a dolphin, one of the most intelligent animals in the ocean.

Although dolphins spend their whole lives in water, they are not fish. They are mammals, like people. They breathe air, they are warm-blooded, and their babies drink milk.

Because it needs air, a dolphin must swim to the surface many times every hour. It breathes through a blowhole on top of its head. In one quick puff, it pushes out old air and pulls in fresh air. Then it can dive again and hold its breath for several minutes.

A baby dolphin is called a calf. Soon after birth, its mother guides it to the surface for its first breath. The calf drinks her rich milk and stays by her side for three to six years while it learns to hunt.

Dolphins live in groups called pods. Members of a pod often work together. For example, they may swim in a circle around a school of fish, pushing the fish into a tight ball that is easy to catch.

Dolphins can find food even in dark or cloudy water by using echolocation. A dolphin sends out quick clicks. When the clicks hit an object, they bounce back as echoes. From these echoes, the dolphin can tell where the object is, how big it is, and even what shape it has.

Each dolphin also has a signature whistle. This sound works like a name, and other dolphins in the pod learn it.

Dolphins sleep in an unusual way. Only half of the brain rests at a time, and one eye often stays open. As a result, the dolphin can keep breathing and watch for danger.

Sadly, many dolphins get trapped in fishing nets, and plastic trash can make them sick. Protecting the sea helps protect these clever swimmers.

versions.text:
On a calm morning in the Red Sea, a gray fin slices through the waves, and a moment later a streamlined animal leaps high into the air before landing with a splash. It is a dolphin, one of the most intelligent creatures in the ocean.

Afterward, it can dive again and hold its breath for several minutes.

A newborn dolphin is called a calf. Shortly after birth, its mother guides it to the surface for its very first breath. The calf drinks her nutritious milk and remains beside her for three to six years, gradually learning how to hunt and how to avoid predators.

Dolphins live in social groups called pods, and members of a pod frequently cooperate when they hunt. For instance, several dolphins may encircle a school of fish, herding the fish into a tight ball that is considerably easier to catch.

A dolphin produces rapid clicks that travel through the water, and when the clicks strike an object, they bounce back as echoes. By interpreting these echoes, the dolphin can determine where the object is located, how large it is, and even what shape it has.

Each dolphin also develops its own signature whistle. This distinctive sound functions like a name, and other members of the pod learn to recognize it.

Dolphins sleep in a remarkable manner. Only one half of the brain rests at a time, and one eye often stays open. Consequently, the dolphin can continue breathing and remain alert to potential danger.

versions.title: Dolphins: Smart Swimmers
versions.text:
On a tranquil morning in the Red Sea, a gray dorsal fin slices through the waves, and a moment later a streamlined animal launches itself into the air before plunging back into the water. It is a dolphin, a member of one of the most intelligent groups of animals on Earth.

Although dolphins spend their entire lives in the ocean, they are not fish but mammals, which means they breathe air, maintain a warm body temperature, and nourish their offspring with milk. Unlike fish, which sweep their tails from side to side, dolphins propel themselves by moving their powerful tail flukes up and down.

Because it depends on atmospheric oxygen, a dolphin must return to the surface many times every hour. It breathes through a blowhole on the top of its head, which allows it to exhale stale air and inhale fresh air in a fraction of a second. It can then dive again and hold its breath for several minutes.

A newborn dolphin, called a calf, usually emerges tail first, and its mother immediately guides it to the surface for its first breath. The calf drinks her fat-rich milk and remains beside her for three to six years, gradually acquiring the skills it needs to hunt and to avoid predators.

Dolphins live in social groups known as pods, and members frequently cooperate while hunting. Several dolphins may encircle a school of fish, herding them into a tightly packed ball that the group can then feed on together.

Even in murky water, dolphins can locate prey through echolocation. A dolphin produces rapid clicks that travel through the water, and when the clicks strike an object, echoes return to the dolphin. By interpreting these echoes, the dolphin can determine an object's distance, size, and shape.

Each dolphin also develops a signature whistle during its first months of life. This distinctive sound functions much like a name, and other members of the pod recognize and sometimes imitate it.

Dolphins sleep in an extraordinary manner: one hemisphere of the brain rests while the other remains active, and one eye often stays open. Consequently, the animal can continue breathing and remain alert to danger.

Unfortunately, thousands of dolphins die every year as bycatch, accidentally caught in fishing nets meant for other species, while plastic pollution creates additional hazards. Protecting the ocean therefore protects these remarkable swimmers as well.

versions.title: Dolphins: Smart Swimmers
versions.text:
On a tranquil morning in the Red Sea, a gray dorsal fin slices through the waves, and a moment later a streamlined animal launches itself into the air before plunging gracefully back into the water. The animal is a dolphin, a member of one of the most intelligent and socially sophisticated groups of animals on Earth, whose abilities continue to fascinate marine biologists.

Although dolphins spend their entire lives in the ocean, they are not fish but mammals, which means they breathe atmospheric air, maintain a consistently warm body temperature, and nourish their offspring with milk. Unlike fish, which propel themselves by sweeping their tails horizontally, dolphins generate thrust by moving their muscular tail flukes vertically.

Because it depends on atmospheric oxygen, a dolphin must return to the surface repeatedly every hour. It breathes through a blowhole positioned on the top of its head, which enables it to exhale stale air and inhale fresh air in a fraction of a second, after which it can submerge again and remain underwater for several minutes.

A newborn dolphin, called a calf, usually emerges tail first, and its mother immediately escorts it to the surface for its initial breath. The calf consumes her exceptionally fat-rich milk and remains beside her for three to six years, gradually acquiring the specialized skills necessary for cooperative hunting and for evading predators.

Dolphins inhabit social groups known as pods, and their members frequently cooperate while hunting. Several individuals may encircle a school of fish, herding the terrified prey into a densely concentrated ball on which the entire group can subsequently feed efficiently.

Even in murky water, dolphins can locate prey through echolocation, a remarkably precise biological sonar system. A dolphin generates rapid clicks that travel through the surrounding water, and whenever these clicks strike an object, echoes return to the dolphin. By interpreting the returning echoes, the animal can calculate an object's distance, dimensions, and approximate shape.

Each dolphin additionally develops a signature whistle during its first months of life, and this distinctive vocalization functions much like a personal name, since other members of the pod recognize, remember, and occasionally imitate it when communicating.

Dolphins sleep in an extraordinary manner: one hemisphere of the brain rests while the other remains active, and one eye frequently stays open, so that the animal can continue breathing voluntarily and remain vigilant against potential danger.

Unfortunately, thousands of dolphins perish annually as bycatch, accidentally captured in commercial fishing nets intended for other species, while plastic pollution introduces additional environmental hazards. Conserving the marine environment therefore safeguards these remarkable swimmers as well.

keyWords.example: Saudi Arabia is located in the Northern Hemisphere.

keyWords.definition: animals that are caught by accident in nets meant for other kinds of fish
keyWords.example: New net designs helped reduce the bycatch of sea turtles.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Dolphins are dangerous predators that often threaten fishing boats and the people on them.
Echolocation is the only skill that makes dolphins intelligent.
Dolphins should be kept in aquariums for their protection.
Dolphins are intelligent mammals with remarkable adaptations, yet people threaten them.
questions.why: The article covers breathing, raising calves, cooperative hunting, echolocation, signature whistles, sleep, and human threats.

wrong.A: The article describes dolphins hunting fish, not threatening boats.
wrong.B: Echolocation is one of several abilities described.

questions.stem: According to the article, how is a dolphin calf usually born?
options: Head first, inside a nest
Tail first, and then guided to the surface
In shallow water on the beach
From an egg that its mother lays on the sea floor
questions.why: The article says a calf usually emerges tail first and its mother guides it to the surface for its first breath.

wrong.A: Dolphins do not build nests, and the article says tail first.
wrong.C: The article does not mention beaches.
wrong.D: Dolphins are mammals and do not lay eggs at all.

questions.stem: When does a dolphin develop its signature whistle?
options: When it becomes the leader of its pod
Only after it is caught in a net
During its first months of life
When it begins to sleep with one eye open
questions.why: The article states that each dolphin develops its signature whistle during its first months of life.

wrong.A: The article does not link the whistle to leadership.
wrong.B: Nets are a threat, not a cause of whistles.
wrong.D: Sleep is unrelated to when the whistle develops.

questions.stem: In the article, the word bycatch refers to —
options: dolphins caught by accident in nets meant for other species
the many fish that a whole pod of dolphins catches together
plastic that floats on the sea
a game that calves play
questions.why: The article defines bycatch as dolphins accidentally captured in nets intended for other species.

wrong.B: Fish caught on purpose by the pod are prey, not bycatch.
wrong.C: Plastic pollution is a separate hazard.

questions.stem: What is the result of one hemisphere of a dolphin's brain staying active during sleep?
options: The dolphin dreams about hunting.
The dolphin's tail moves side to side.
The dolphin can no longer hear the echoes of its own clicks.
The dolphin can keep breathing and stay alert to danger.
questions.why: The article says that because one hemisphere stays active, the dolphin can continue breathing and remain alert.

wrong.B: Dolphins move their tails up and down.
wrong.C: The article does not say sleep blocks hearing.

questions.stem: Why can't a dolphin sleep as deeply as a human does?
options: It must stay in the warm sunlight.
It must consciously come up to breathe, so part of its brain must stay awake.
It must keep hunting fish with the other members of its pod all through the night.
Its calves sleep only during the day.
questions.why: Dolphins breathe voluntarily and need air from the surface, so complete deep sleep could stop them from breathing.

wrong.A: Sunlight has nothing to do with sleep in the article.
wrong.C: The article does not say dolphins hunt all night; the reason is breathing.
wrong.D: Calves' sleep schedule is not described.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might a pod find more food than a dolphin hunting alone?
options: Dolphins in pods have louder whistles.
Single dolphins cannot use echolocation.
By cooperating, the dolphins can herd fish into a tight ball.
Pods only hunt in clear water.
questions.why: The article explains that several dolphins encircle a school and herd the fish into a packed ball the whole group can eat.

wrong.A: Whistles identify dolphins; volume is not linked to food.
wrong.D: Echolocation lets dolphins hunt even in murky water.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare a dolphin's tail movement with a fish's?
options: To prove that dolphins swim slower than fish
To argue that fish are more intelligent
To explain how fish breathe
To give another piece of evidence that dolphins are mammals, not fish
questions.why: The comparison appears in the paragraph explaining that dolphins are mammals, adding a visible difference from fish.

wrong.B: The article does not compare intelligence with fish.

HIGH.prompt: Which dolphin adaptation do you think is most important for its survival: breathing through a blowhole, echolocation, or half-brain sleep? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
